--- title: "Nets and dn0" --- A net enters the models as two numbers: `dn0_use`, the probability that a mosquito is killed when it contacts a treated net, and `itn_use`, the share of the population sleeping under one. Which insecticide the net carries, and how resistant the local mosquitoes have become, is compressed entirely into `dn0_use`. `calculate_dn0` does that compression, and it is the first call in almost every `estimint` workflow. ## Net types Four formulations are modelled, and `net_types` returns their canonical names, alphabetically. ::: {#38f381bc .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import net_types, calculate_dn0 net_types() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['pyrethroid_only', 'pyrethroid_pbo', 'pyrethroid_ppf', 'pyrethroid_pyrrole'] ``` ::: ::: Each has a short alias, accepted anywhere a net type is, and the aliases double as the keyword-argument names in the wider API. | Alias | Canonical name | Formulation | |---|---|---| | `py_only` | `pyrethroid_only` | Pyrethroid alone | | `py_pbo` | `pyrethroid_pbo` | Pyrethroid with PBO | | `py_ppf` | `pyrethroid_ppf` | Pyrethroid with pyriproxyfen | | `py_pyrrole` | `pyrethroid_pyrrole` | Pyrethroid with chlorfenapyr | Both spellings are case-insensitive, and the canonical names use underscores throughout. A hyphen raises `ValueError: unknown net type`. ## From a net mix to dn0 `calculate_dn0` takes a resistance level and the net mix as keyword arguments, where each keyword is a net type and each value is the share of the population using that net. ::: {#113f4b87 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} net = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=0.70) net ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` DN0Result(dn0=0.3110000000000001, itn_use=0.7) ``` ::: ::: The return value is a `DN0Result`, a named tuple of exactly two fields. It unpacks and attribute-accesses alike. ::: {#3f71e7eb .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} net.dn0, net.itn_use ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (0.3110000000000001, 0.7) ``` ::: ::: At 30% pyrethroid resistance, a pyrethroid-only net kills about 31% of the mosquitoes that contact it. Coverage is 70%. A mix is expressed by passing more than one net type. Here 40% of the population has pyrethroid-only nets and 30% has PBO nets. The remaining 30% has no net at all. ::: {#64905a23 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} mix = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=0.40, py_pbo=0.30) mix ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` DN0Result(dn0=0.38555000000000006, itn_use=0.7) ``` ::: ::: ## The weighted average and the sum The two fields are constructed differently, and conflating them is the most common error in the package. `dn0` is the **usage-weighted average** of the per-net-type `dn0` values across the mix, which makes it a property of the nets that exist rather than of how many people happen to have them. The weights are normalised. Reconstruct it by hand. ::: {#f7e75b44 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} only = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=1.0).dn0 pbo = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_pbo=1.0).dn0 by_hand = (0.40 * only + 0.30 * pbo) / (0.40 + 0.30) round(by_hand, 5), round(mix.dn0, 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (0.38555, 0.38555) ``` ::: ::: `itn_use` is the **sum** of the shares, 0.40 + 0.30 = 0.70, and it is the total ITN coverage of the population. It is already complete. ::: {.callout-warning} ## `itn_use` is already the coverage `DN0Result.itn_use` is the finished coverage figure, not a weight awaiting a coverage term, so multiplying it by a usage fraction a second time understates the coverage. The error is silent. ::: {#5107dec2 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} net = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=0.70) net.itn_use, round(net.itn_use * 0.70, 3) # the second value is the mistake ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (0.7, 0.49) ``` ::: ::: The model then reads a district with 49% net coverage rather than 70%, and understates the EIR. The size of that error is measured in [Estimating EIR from prevalence](estimating-eir.qmd). ::: ## Resistance and dn0 Holding usage at 1.0 isolates the resistance response of each formulation. ::: {#49eecfd6 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd levels = [0.0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0] table = pd.DataFrame( { f"{r:.2f}": [calculate_dn0(r, **{nt: 1.0}).dn0 for nt in net_types()] for r in levels }, index=net_types(), ).round(4) table.index.name = "net type" table ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00
net type
pyrethroid_only 0.3376 0.3163 0.2850 0.2344 0.0000
pyrethroid_pbo 0.5094 0.4893 0.4567 0.3916 0.0714
pyrethroid_ppf 0.4111 0.3980 0.3777 0.3394 0.1085
pyrethroid_pyrrole 0.5611 0.5526 0.5371 0.4964 0.1522
``` ::: ::: Read across a row for the decay of one formulation, and down a column to compare formulations at a fixed resistance. The `dn0` of a pyrethroid-only net falls to zero at full resistance, while the other three retain some lethality across the whole range. Pyrrole nets are both the most lethal and the flattest, losing only about a tenth of their `dn0` between resistance 0.0 and 0.75, where a pyrethroid-only net loses nearly a third. PPF nets have a low `dn0` throughout the table, because their effect on the next generation is not represented in `dn0` at all and appears only in the scenario pipeline. The resistance-to-`dn0` curves come from the same published source that `malariasimulation` uses. ## A caveat `dn0` summarises the kill on contact and nothing else, so it captures neither repellence nor the loss of a net to wear and disuse over a campaign. The resistance level you supply should be the local pyrethroid resistance at the decision point, and a single net mix is assumed to hold across the population. ## Next - [Estimating EIR from prevalence](estimating-eir.qmd) — feed `dn0_use` and `itn_use` into the inversion. - [Interventions and nets](../03-concepts/interventions.qmd) — the epidemiology behind the four formulations.
